rows.explanation: Behavior is scattered across layered roots and adds a repository port plus one use-case wrapper per CRUD operation. Runtime channels, server-derived auth with scoped authorization, and private row mapping are otherwise coherent. Arithmetic: 6 - 1 = 5.

The design avoids speculative operations and uses the required runtime channels with server-side authentication and RLS. However, labels behavior is split across app and a generic lib bucket, and the combined lib/labels.ts server repository/product-types module does not clearly prevent browser imports of server internals. Arithmetic: 7 - 1 = 6.

The design avoids ports and pass-through use cases, selects the correct runtime channels, derives identity server-side, and keeps provider mapping in a server-only data module. Behavior is scattered across multiple architectural roots, and define-boundary.ts is a universal boundary/result wrapper. Arithmetic: 8 - 1 = 7.

Labels behavior is colocated under src/modules/labels while route-specific glue stays in app. It omits unnecessary operations and ports, uses direct RSC reads, GET browser reads, and top-level Server Actions, derives authentication server-side with RLS authorization, and privately maps provider rows. Arithmetic: 10 - 0 = 10.
Cohesive labels capability with only route glue in app, direct local-store CRUD, correct RSC/GET/Action channels, server-derived auth plus RLS, and private row mapping. No rubric penalties.

Uses the correct runtime channels and avoids speculative ports or operation wrappers. Colocation and server-internal isolation are only partial because behavior is split between app and a generic lib bucket, and the repository is not explicitly server-only. The generic lib bucket incurs the fourth penalty.

Runtime channels, authentication, authorization, and private mapping are coherent. However, labels behavior is scattered across architecture-wide roots and routed through boundary/use-case entries despite being simple CRUD. The generic universal boundary and mandatory layered structure incur penalties.

Correctly separates RSC reads, browser GET reads, and Server Action writes, with explicit server-side auth and private provider mapping. It fails the small-CRUD architecture criteria by scattering the capability across many layer roots and adding a speculative repository port plus one forwarding use-case file per operation.

The framework-neutral operation, provider port, cancellation, idle timeout, commit-aware SSE failure handling, and provider redaction are clear. However, assistant behavior is scattered across generic top-level layers rather than colocated under one capability root. Its shared generic boundary/result wrapper spans stream and job handling, weakening native channel contracts and violating the universal-wrapper prohibition.

The capability is coherently colocated apart from justified runtime entrypoints. It defines a framework-neutral use case and capability-owned provider port, uses a dedicated SSE Route Handler with abort propagation and per-read idle timeout, handles failures differently before and after commitment, preserves channel-native HTTP/SSE/job outcomes, and contains provider details in infrastructure.

The proposal correctly uses a framework-neutral generation use case, provider seam, dedicated SSE route, abort propagation, idle timeout, post-commit error events, and provider-safe contracts. Its files are scattered across generic application/domain/infrastructure roots, and it explicitly shares a generic result/event wrapper across HTTP, stream, and job. Although adapters perform separate mappings, that universal wrapper violates the rubric.

The design colocates assistant behavior under a capability root with justified Route Handler and worker surfaces. It provides a framework-neutral application boundary and capability-shaped provider port, correctly specifies cancellation, idle-only timeout, and commit-sensitive SSE failures, preserves native HTTP/stream/job contracts while sharing semantic primitives, and confines provider data and errors to the adapter.

Strong SSE and job lifecycle design with safe normalized contracts and transport-specific orchestration. However, capability files are scattered across application, domain, infrastructure, and jobs rather than colocated under one capability root, and the provider abstraction is described but no explicit application-owned port is placed in the tree.

The framework-neutral operation, explicit provider port, native channel contracts, failure taxonomy, and provider-safe types are coherent. The capability is dispersed across many top-level architectural folders, and the proposed Route Handler is placed under src/adapters rather than an App Router app/**/route.ts runtime surface or an explicit re-export from one.

Clearly satisfies the required Route Handler/SSE lifecycle, cancellation propagation, idle-gap timeout, post-commit failure event, report-once ownership, provider seam, and job decisions. Its main rubric shortcoming is placement: assistant behavior is distributed across domain, use-cases, adapters, infrastructure, UI, and app roots instead of one capability root.

Provides a coherent capability-rooted design with only the justified App Router and page runtime surfaces outside the module. It uses a framework-neutral generation operation and application-owned provider port, preserves SSE and job-native lifecycles, propagates abort, implements an idle rather than total timeout, changes failure representation after commit, reports unexpected failures at channel boundaries, and prevents provider details from leaking.

The board capability clearly owns orchestration and policy, consumes narrow trusted capability surfaces, preserves an acyclic graph, exposes a board RSC entrypoint to the route, and centralizes unexpected-failure reporting while enforcing capability and board authorization.

The board use-case owns the cross-capability workflow through board-local ports, with independent trusted readers and a thin RSC route. Authorization is coherent, but the proposal does not clearly guarantee that an unexpected failure is reported exactly once.

The board slice owns policy, preserves capability independence, provides a board-specific RSC path, and explicitly centralizes reporting once. Its dependency design is only partial against the rubric because it rejects board-owned ports and has the board operation call published foreign application operations directly.

Capability APIs remain independent and enforce their own authorization, while the route-local workflow applies board policy and handles failures safely. However, board orchestration is owned by route-private code rather than a board capability, and the RSC route does not consume a board RSC/public capability surface.

Board policy and orchestration live in the route rather than a board capability/public RSC surface. The route uses narrow trusted capability APIs and preserves an acyclic graph, but it defines no board-owned ports and does not specify single-point unexpected-error reporting. The claim that label reads run in parallel while requiring IDs from the work-item result is also internally inconsistent.

A board slice clearly owns policy and orchestration; the route uses a board read adapter, capability boundaries remain independent, authorization is layered, and unexpected failures are normalized and reported once. Credit is partial for board-owned dependencies because it deliberately omits board-language ports and directly consumes capability operation surfaces.

The board use case owns all cross-capability policy, defines narrow board ports, and uses adapters over public actor-scoped capability contracts. The RSC route invokes a board DAL entrypoint, dependencies remain acyclic, inaccessible labels are excluded without disclosure, and unexpected failures are reported once.

The board capability cleanly owns orchestration and policy, with board-language ports wired to narrow trusted server APIs. The route imports the board RSC surface, work-items and labels remain independent, authorization is enforced at each owning boundary, inaccessible labels produce a typed rejection, and unexpected failures are reported once.
